directions: This patented sport of common trumpet vine is grown for its bold pinwheel leaves streaked heavily in creamy white rather than for a different flower color, since blooms remain the typical orange-red trumpets of the species. Give it a sturdy arbor, fence, or wall to climb, since its aerial rootlets can damage wood siding or mortar over time. Full sun brings out the strongest variegation and the best flowering; shadier sites cause the foliage to revert toward plain green. Cut the vine back hard in late winter each year to control its vigorous size and to stimulate fresh, brightly variegated new growth.

Discovered growing on a Georgia fence, this hybrid trumpet vine begins its bold clusters of orange-red, yellow-throated trumpets earlier in late spring than most tagliabuana selections and continues sporadically until frost. It is an extremely vigorous woody twiner that can add many feet of growth in a single season, so plant it only where a large arbor, pergola, or sturdy fence can support its eventual bulk. It tolerates poor, dry soils once established and needs little supplemental water, but an annual hard pruning in late winter keeps it from overwhelming its structure. Hummingbirds are drawn to it in large numbers throughout the bloom season.
sources: University of Georgia Research Foundation Plant Patent PP19415

directions: Selected from a naturally occurring plant found growing wild on Balboa Island in coastal California, this cultivar bears unusually large, uniformly scarlet-red trumpet flowers held in generous clusters against dark green pinnate foliage. Like other trumpet vines it climbs by clinging aerial roots and needs a sturdy arbor, pergola, or masonry wall rather than wood siding, which it can damage. It blooms most heavily in full sun on new wood produced each season, so prune it back hard in late winter to renew growth and keep its size in check. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well and reliably attract hummingbirds through summer and fall.

This European-bred, plant-breeders'-rights-protected trumpet vine produces abundant large, warm orange trumpet flowers over a long midsummer season while staying noticeably more restrained in overall size than typical trumpet vine selections, reaching roughly ten feet rather than sprawling widely. That more compact habit makes it a better fit for a modest trellis, mailbox post, or large container than most Campsis. Give it full sun and a sturdy support to twine on, and prune it back each spring to maintain a tidy shape and encourage strong new flowering wood. It tolerates poor soils and needs little supplemental watering once established.

This is the true dwarf form of Asiatic jasmine, staying only a few inches tall while its wiry stems trail and root as they spread, quickly knitting together into a dense weed-smothering mat. Small glossy leaves take on a bronze to reddish tinge in cool weather, adding winter interest that the plain species lacks. Space plants closely for fast coverage under trees, along slopes, or as a lawn substitute in areas too shady or difficult to mow. It tolerates both considerable sun and fairly deep shade once established and needs only occasional watering during dry spells. An early spring mowing or shearing on a high deck keeps the planting even and encourages fresh, dense new growth.

Grown as much for its ever-shifting foliage as for its fragrant white pinwheel flowers, this star jasmine selection unfurls new leaves in shades of pink before they pass through cream and green and finally flush burgundy-red once cool weather arrives, so the vine looks different through much of the year. It twines readily on a trellis, fence, or mailbox post, or can be kept low and mounded as a groundcover with occasional pinching. Plant it in full sun for the boldest color change and the heaviest bloom, and water regularly the first year or two while the root system establishes. Once settled it tolerates short dry spells but performs best with even moisture.

This selection of our native coral honeysuckle carries blue-green foliage and an especially long, dense flush of slender red tubular flowers from late spring well into fall, drawing hummingbirds throughout the growing season. It twines rather than climbing by holdfasts, so give it a mailbox post, trellis, or wire support to wrap around. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle it is well-behaved and non-aggressive, making it a good native substitute for that weedy look. Plant in full sun for the most flowers, water regularly while it establishes, and prune lightly right after the first big flush to encourage further rebloom.
